mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Taaroa ‌place ​creator, supreme ​being ​at ​the center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Taaroa ‌appears ​in polynesian ‌tradition ​as creator, ​supreme ​being. ​The name's ​meaning, ‌"The ​distant one", ‌shapes ​the narratives ‌told ​about ‌this figure.

### ​Worship ‌and ​Memory (Cult)

​Devotees ‌and later ‌tradition-keepers ‌preserved ​Taaroa in ​ritual, ‌text, ​and iconography, ​ensuring ‌the name ​survived ​into ‌the modern ​scholarly ‌record.

​The myths ​of ​Taaroa survive ​in ‌fragments, ‌summaries, and ​later ‌retellings. ​Each version ​reflects ‌the interests ‌of ‌its ‌tellers — ​poets, ‌priests, ​philosophers, and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does ​not privilege ​a ‌single ​version; it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Taaroa ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

overview.body:
**Taaroa** ​(*taaroa*) — ‌Creator, Supreme ‌Being ​· The ​distant one ​— belongs ​to ​the Polynesian ‌tradition, where ​it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Creator, Supreme ​Being". The ‌name ​means "The ​distant one"[^1].

​In the ​old ​religion of ‌Tahiti, **Taaroa** ​is ‌not one ​god among ‌many ​but the ‌ground of ​all ‌divinity — ​the **self-existent ​one** who ‌dwelt ‌alone in ‌the primal ​darkness, ​burst the ‌shell of ​his ​own being ‌to make ​sky ​and earth, ‌and fathered ​or simply ‌is ​every other ​god. The ​first ​missionary scholars ‌recorded his ‌cosmogony ​with respect ‌verging on ​awe.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**Taaroa** ‌and serves ​its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/taaroa/). ​The displayed ​form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description ​computed from ‌the displayed ​form itself. ​The ​plain ASCII ‌form *taaroa* ​contains ‌the same ​letters: no ‌recovered ​diacritics or ‌special encoding ‌is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​modern ​Polynesian orthographies; ​macron ​usage ​follows each ‌tradition’s ​reference ​dictionaries. Etymologically ‌the ​name ‌means "The ​distant ‌one"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Taaroa** ​matches the ​conventional ‌scholarly ​romanization. The ‌plain ​ASCII ‌form *taaroa* ​contains ‌the ​same letters, ‌so ​no ​lost diacritics ‌or ‌encoding ‌transition is ​claimed. ​The ‌editorial work ​is ​to ‌fix one ​reviewed ​reference ‌spelling, preserve ​capitalization ‌and ​provenance, and ​keep ​the ​original evidence ‌visible. ‌The ​displayed form ‌is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— a ‌description ‌computed ‌from the ‌displayed ​form ‌itself.

meditation.body:
Most creation ​stories start ‌with a problem: ‌chaos to ​be fought, ​a dragon to ​be split, ​a rival to ​be overthrown. ‌Taaroa's story ​starts with something ​rarer — ‌**sufficiency**. Before there ​was anything, ‌there was ​a being who ‌needed nothing: ​no parents, no ​materials, no ​opponent. The ​world is not ​a conquest ‌but an overflow, ​the cracking ‌of a shell ​that had ‌become too ​small for the ‌being inside ​it. And there ‌is a ​loneliness in ​this that the ‌myth does ‌not hide: the ‌first thing ​the god ​does in the ‌darkness is ​call out, and ​no one ‌answers. Creation, ​on this reading, ​is not ‌an act of ​power but ‌of company — ​the universe ​as the ​solution to solitude.

​When the ‌work is done, ‌Ta'aroa withdraws ​to the ‌highest heaven and ​leaves the ​world to his ‌children. Power ‌that creates ‌and then steps ‌back is ​the most difficult ‌kind to ​imagine, and ​the Tahitians imagined ​it — ‌a supreme being ​whose supremacy ​consists in having ​delegated everything ‌and in ​being, still, the ​direction of ​every prayer. That ‌is a ​theology of ‌confidence: the maker ​does not ‌need to manage, ​because the ‌making was ‌perfect. The name ​Ta'aroa, with ​its gentle glottal ​catch like ​a held ‌breath, is the ‌sound of ​that confidence.[^1]
